objective.value: Test how flame-retardant-treated cotton textiles burn and self-extinguish in microgravity, and compare the results with the terrestrial upward-burning screening test. The stated hypothesis is that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well if not better than the same material in normal gravity with other conditions (pressure, oxygen concentration, temperature) identical.

sources.note: NASA BASS document (BASS-M section): tests ten treated textiles at various air flow rates, evaluates each textile's self-extinguishment, and compares microgravity results to the terrestrial upward-burning screen; states the microgravity burning hypothesis

NASA BASS document: NASA selects spacecraft materials from ground flammability tests; BASS-M measures how low gravity changes a textile's flame-retardant behaviour, improving procedures for testing new materials
Challenge brief: prevention is achieved through material selection, which depends on understanding flammability limits

safety_functions.note: Deduced, not labelled by the source: the experiment supports material selection / flammability screening, which the brief defines as prevention.

sources.note: NASA BASS document: BASS-M consists of textile samples; space-based burning and flame extinguishment tests on cotton textiles

value: cotton textiles treated with flame retardants
untreated cotton textile (control and igniter piece)

sources.note: NASA BASS document: 44 textile samples, four of each of eleven textile types, one set untreated controls; ten treated textiles; the untreated piece is ignited and its flame impinges on the adjacent treated textile

fuel_geometry.value: Flat textile coupons. Each treated sample is paired with a small adjacent untreated textile piece that is ignited by an integrated hot-wire igniter, and the flame impinges on the treated textile. A magazine report puts the samples at about 1 cm by 3 cm.

sources.note: NASA BASS document: each sample set has a small untreated textile ignited by an integrated hot wire igniter, with the flame impinging on the immediately adjacent treated textile
Smithsonian Air & Space magazine article: BASS-M small samples are about one centimeter by three centimeters (secondary source, not NASA/PSI)

fuel_geometry.note: The arrangement is stated in the NASA BASS document; the 1 cm x 3 cm size comes only from a secondary magazine article.

sources.note: NASA BASS document: BASS-M is conducted inside the sealed MSG work volume on the ISS

apparatus.value: Slightly modified Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) hardware: a small flow duct with an igniter and a small nozzle, exchangeable textile samples, a fan that produces a co-flow of air through the duct, and integrated hot-wire igniters.

sources.note: NASA BASS document: BASS-M utilises slightly modified SPICE hardware in the MSG; the crew installs SPICE and BASS hardware consisting of a small flow duct with an igniter and a small nozzle, exchangeable textile samples, and a fan producing a co-flow of air

Miller & Fletcher, 'Topical: Spacecraft Materials Fire Safety' (2023-2032 decadal survey): the BASS series of experiments were limited to 1 atmosphere and oxygen concentrations below 22% due to MSG constraints

o2_percent.note: Group statement for the BASS series (BASS, BASS-II, BASS-M) under MSG constraints; only the upper bound (below 22%) is stated, so min is null. No BASS-M-specific oxygen range was found.

sources.note: Miller & Fletcher decadal-survey topical: the BASS series of experiments were limited to 1 atmosphere due to MSG constraints

pressure_psi.note: Group statement for the BASS series. Only the upper bound (1 atmosphere) is stated; converted to psi (1 atm = 14.7 psi) and the lower bound left null. No BASS-M-specific pressure was found.

sources.note: NASA BASS document (BASS-M protocol): a fan produces a co-flow of air through the duct, an anemometer measures the actual flow rate, and the crew member adjusts the airflow from 5 to 50 cm/s

airflow.note: Stated for the BASS-M textile tests.

sources.note: NASA BASS document: BASS-M is a microgravity observation of burning solid materials on board the ISS; the exact g level is not stated
Challenge brief: low-gravity combustion experiments conducted on the ISS

gravity_g.note: ISS platform treated as microgravity (~0 g).

diluents.note: No chamber diluent is stated for BASS-M. Unlike the BASS and BASS-II protocols, the BASS-M protocol in the NASA BASS document does not describe a nitrogen suppressant or glovebox nitrogen vitiation, so diluents were left unknown rather than inferred from the other BASS investigations.

value: Textile material (ten treated flame-retardant cotton textiles plus untreated controls)

sources.note: NASA BASS document: BASS-M tests ten different treated textiles at various air flow rates; 44 sample test points

held_constant.note: Sources describe the varied variables but do not enumerate the conditions held constant across BASS-M tests. The hypothesis names pressure, oxygen concentration and temperature as conditions expected to be identical, but this is a hypothesis statement, not a recorded held-constant list.

sources.note: NASA BASS document: an anemometer measures the actual flow rate and a radiometer measures flame output; data is downlinked by video during or after each flame test and digital still photos are downlinked after selected tests

relevance_notes.value: Directly targets spacecraft material selection: it measures how low gravity changes the flame-retardant behaviour of real cotton textiles and compares microgravity self-extinguishment with the terrestrial upward-burning screen (worst-case geometry on Earth), which underpins NASA-STD-6001-based material screening.

sources.note: NASA BASS document (BASS-M): compares microgravity results to the terrestrial upward burning used to screen materials; NASA selects materials from ground tests that do not consider microgravity effects
Miller & Fletcher decadal-survey topical: standard material screening uses the NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 upward flame spread test, whose conservatism for microgravity is uncertain
